title: Where is God?
hookLine: the Kotzker rebbe: God dwells wherever we let Him in

cards: Where is God? Up in the sky? In the synagogue?
Everywhere? It's the kind of question a child asks at bedtime, and one quick answer is always ready: everywhere. It's a good answer.

It's even in the Bible. But one Hasidic rebbe, well-known for being fierce, blunt and impossible to please, heard that answer from a room full of learned men, and told them they had it only half right.

teach.b: Menachem Mendel of Kotzk was a Hasidic rebbe in Poland, known for a hatred of anything fake. He wanted truth, all of it, and he could be harsh about it.
The story goes that he once surprised a group of learned guests with a question: where does God live? They laughed. What a thing to ask!

teach.h: THE WHOLE EARTH IS FULL OF GLORY.
teach.b: The angels call out: "the whole earth is full of His glory." The rebbe answered his own question.
God lives wherever people let Him in. He isn't denying the verse. The whole earth may be full of glory, but a person can walk right through it and notice nothing.
You can stand in a beautiful place and be somewhere else entirely: inside your phone, your worry, your pride. The door opens from the inside.

In the Kedushah said on Shabbat and festivals, the congregation says Isaiah's line, and a little later the prayer pictures the angels asking each other: where is the place of His glory? Ayeh mekom kevodo.
The answer comes from Ezekiel's vision: blessed be the glory of the Lord from His place.
The question sits right next to the answer. Jewish tradition holds both at once: God fills the world, and God can feel absent. For the Kotzker, what closes the distance isn't a map or a building.
It's a person who stops pretending, and makes room for something larger.

how: In the Kedushah, said aloud in the synagogue's repetition of the Amidah, the congregation proclaims Isaiah's line that the whole earth is full of God's glory; the Kotzker's saying is often quoted in sermons on sincerity.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the whole earth is full of His glory

s: the Kotzker says Isaiah's verse is wrong
he doesn't deny it. he says a person must still let God in.
the Kedushah holds both 'full of His glory' and 'where is the place of His glory?'
Jewish prayer keeps the answer and the question side by side.
the Kotzker was known for gentle, easygoing answers
he was well-known for fierce honesty and a hatred of anything fake.

games.q: the rebbe asks a room of scholars: where does God live? what do they say?
o: everywhere. the whole earth is full of His glory.
games.why: they laugh and quote Isaiah. the rebbe answers: wherever people let Him in.

practice: Notice where you're closed right now: rushing, guarded, carrying a grudge, or pretending everything is fine. Don't force anything open; just loosen one latch, breathe into the tight place, and leave a little room.
If you pray, invite God in, in your own words or with Isaiah's line; if you don't, let the room fill with whatever is good and true right here.

wordCard.voice: Kotzker, nickname for Menachem Mendel of Kotzk. His answer to where is God: wherever people let Him in. The earth is full of glory, and the door opens from the inside.

orig.note: Hebrew: where is the place of His glory? A line said in the Kedushah.

carryVoice: Your line: wherever you let him in. The glory is already here; the latch is on your side. See you tomorrow.
